synth.title: Information architecture and navigation
synth.principle_summary: Navigation cost is the sum of two separable things, and folk rules that count clicks instead conflate them: a scent cost (does the label or title predict the destination before the user commits, per Pirolli and Card's information foraging theory) and a consistency cost (does an identical control, especially back, behave the same on every screen, per Nielsen's heuristic 4). Depth in taps or clicks is not itself the cost function; Porter's 2003 study (already flagged MYTH in Solen's folklore table) found no drop in task success past three clicks when scent stayed strong across paths as long as 25 pages. Breadcrumbs are a wayfinding device that earns its screen space only once "where am I" stops being answerable from the title alone; NN/g's own guideline puts flat 1-2 level hierarchies below that bar. Independently, a five-app competitor teardown and an eight-app pattern scout converge on the same finding without citing any study: not one booking or discovery competitor observed (Fresha, Treatwell, Booksy, Vagaro, Doctolib, Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook, Trip.com, Turo, Air New Zealand, Tripadvisor, Shopee) shows a breadcrumb in its transactional browse-to-book path, and the one clear breadcrumb sighting (Airbnb, a full 6-level trail) lives exclusively in its Help Center, never the booking flow. A single global back control is a consistency bet riding on a platform convention (iOS and Android fix system-back to one place per app), reinforced by the same booking-app set showing zero page-local back exceptions outside a focused wizard flow.

real_world_evidence.source: Fresha, live-browsed 2026-07-22 and separately Mobbin-captured (direct competitor)
real_world_evidence.what: Zero breadcrumb anywhere: search-results screen carries only a sticky search/filter bar, venue-detail carries only a single back chevron over the photo. Bottom tab bar is 3 icons (Home, Search, Bookings), the observed floor of the tab-count range.

A full 6-level breadcrumb (Home > All topics > Searching and booking > Booking places to stay > Booking basics > Booking split stays) exists ONLY inside the Help Center. The transactional booking flow itself stays breadcrumb-free, the sharpest single data point for 'breadcrumbs belong to reference surfaces, not the transactional path.'

real_world_evidence.source: Treatwell, Booksy, Vagaro, Doctolib, competitor teardown 2026-07-22
real_world_evidence.what: All four use flat category-then-location entry (service type, then city), none render a breadcrumb anywhere in their browse or booking flow. Combined with Fresha, n=5 competitors observed, 0 use a breadcrumb transactionally.

real_world_evidence.source: Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook, Trip.com, Turo, Air New Zealand, Tripadvisor, Shopee, Mobbin scout
real_world_evidence.what: Universally one back chevron top-left at the booking-detail/confirmation screen, no breadcrumb, no stacked home-plus-back. Direct convergent support for Solen's single-global-back law at the exact surface it governs.

real_world_evidence.source: Zara, H&M, Anthropologie, DICK'S, Target, Amazon, Mobbin scout
real_world_evidence.what: Category depth is signaled by a top tab strip plus a flat tappable row list plus a back chevron, never a breadcrumb string. Matches the domain's 'title/tab is the landmark, not a crumb trail' mechanic.

real_world_evidence.source: Fresha (3), Klook/Walmart/Gopuff/Swiggy/Burger King (5), Mobbin bottom-tab-count survey
real_world_evidence.what: Observed range across marketplace and booking apps is 3-5 top-level tabs; the category leader most structurally similar to Solen (Fresha) sits at the floor of 3. No app surveyed exceeded 5.

real_world_evidence.source: monday.com and Headspace Support, Mobbin scout
real_world_evidence.what: The only two apps where a breadcrumb DID appear, and both were search-result disambiguation or help-center contexts, never the primary browse/booking flow, matching NN/g's own 'breadcrumbs are secondary nav' framing.

real_world_evidence.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Hamburger Menus vs. Visible Navigation
real_world_evidence.what: 179-participant study: hidden nav was 39% slower on desktop task completion, 21% higher in perceived difficulty, over 20% lower in content discoverability, and 15% slower on mobile, versus visible tab/nav bar for 4-5 or fewer top-level options.

synth.generative_prior: Three concrete defaults, each now grounded in both a cited source and multi-app convergence rather than brand analogy alone. (1) Top-level navigation stays a VISIBLE tab bar of 3-5 destinations, never collapses to a hamburger at that count: NN/g's 179-participant study shows a 15-39% task-time and discoverability penalty for hidden nav, and the observed competitor range is exactly 3 (Fresha, the category-closest competitor) to 5 (Klook, Walmart, Gopuff, Swiggy). (2) A breadcrumb is reserved for genuinely deep or cross-context surfaces (Solen's locked >=2 levels, SOURCE.md:1229), and even then should be treated as a reference/disambiguation device, not a transactional-flow default: zero of 13 real apps surveyed across two independent scouts (5 direct competitors, 8 booking-category peers) show a breadcrumb in their browse-to-book path, and the one clear sighting (Airbnb's 6-level trail) lives only in Help Center. Solen's title-in-header pattern for top-level browse already satisfies this: the title IS the scent cue. (3) A single global back control, top-left, is the default on every screen; page-local back duplicates are the exception reserved for focused wizard flows (e.g. booking). This is now supported not just by the Fitts-Law placement argument (domain 10) and Nielsen's consistency heuristic, but by 8 of 8 booking apps surveyed (Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook, Trip.com, Turo, Air New Zealand, Tripadvisor, Shopee) showing zero exceptions to single, unstacked back navigation at the detail/confirmation screen.
synth.proposed_addition:
## Domain 24: information architecture and navigation (owner-added 2026-07-22, synthesis pass)

Grounds SOURCE.md's breadcrumb-depth rule (V3-D411) and the single-global-back law (project_single_global_back memory) in cited navigation research AND independent multi-app convergence, replacing the prior brand-analogy-only justification. Cross-references domain 1 (Hick's and Fitts's Law) and domain 10 (top-left back placement, already Fitts-grounded) rather than restating them. Cross-references PSYCHOLOGY.md for any habit/retention angle on navigation (e.g. why users return to a persistent tab); that stays in the behavioral layer and is not duplicated here.

Navigation cost decomposes into a scent cost (does the label or title predict the destination before the user commits, Pirolli and Card 1999, Information Foraging, Psychological Review 106, T2) and a consistency cost (does an identical control behave identically everywhere, Nielsen and Molich 1990 / Nielsen 1994 heuristic 4, derived from a factor analysis of 249 usability problems, T2). Click or tap COUNT is not the cost function on its own: Porter's 2003 study (44 users, 620 tasks, 8,000-plus clicks, successful paths as long as 25 pages, no drop in success or satisfaction past three clicks) is already flagged MYTH in Solen's folklore table (RATIONALE.md:252) for exactly this reason, and a parallel "three-tap rule" trope surfaced during this synthesis (UXPin, cited with zero data behind it) should be added to that same folklore table as a second instance of the pattern, not adopted as a number.

**Breadcrumb depth (T2 plus CONV convergence).** NN/g's breadcrumb guideline states flat hierarchies of 1-2 levels do not need one; Solen's locked literal (SOURCE.md:1229, V3-D411) shows a breadcrumb starting one level earlier, at 2+. This tension is recorded, not reopened: the app-register argument (bottom-tab plus back-button plus title, SOURCE.md:1237) already substitutes the header title for level-1 scent, which is a legitimate first-principles reason to show wayfinding one level earlier than a content site would. What synthesis adds on top of the academic source: two independent real-app scouts, thirteen apps total (Fresha, Treatwell, Booksy, Vagaro, Doctolib, Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook, Trip.com, Turo, Air New Zealand, Tripadvisor, Shopee), zero of which show a breadcrumb anywhere in their browse-to-book transactional path. The only breadcrumb sightings across both scouts (monday.com, Headspace Support, and Airbnb's Help Center) were all in search-disambiguation or reference/help contexts, never the primary flow. This upgrades the domain's boundary line from an inference to an observed pattern: a breadcrumb, even where the locked depth threshold technically allows one, reads as more appropriate to a reference or disambiguation surface than to Solen's core search-to-book path, which should keep leaning on title-as-landmark plus single back chevron instead. This does not touch the locked >=2-levels literal; it narrows WHERE that literal should actually fire in practice, a judgment call for whoever next touches a 2+-level surface, not a re-open of the number.

**Visible tab bar over hidden nav (T2, new to this domain).** NN/g's hamburger-menu study (179 participants) found hidden nav costs 39% slower desktop task completion, 21% higher perceived difficulty, over 20% lower content discoverability, and a smaller but present 15% mobile penalty, versus a visible tab/nav bar for up to 4-5 top-level options. This is a caution the prior academic-only draft did not carry: Solen's bottom tab bar should stay visible as the destination count grows, and should not be collapsed into a hamburger as a "cleanup" move even under space pressure. Real-app convergence: the observed range across marketplace and booking apps (Fresha 3, Treatwell/Booksy-style peers, Klook/Walmart/Gopuff/Swiggy/Burger King 5) is 3-5 tabs with no observed app exceeding 5; Fresha, the category-closest competitor, sits at the floor.

**Single global back (T2 heuristic plus CONV platform convention plus CONV observed convergence).** The value of one back control is not primarily its placement (domain 10's Fitts argument) but that a user who learns what back does on one screen should never re-learn it on the next (heuristic 4). Platform convention (Apple HIG, Android Material Design fixing system-back to one place per app) is the delivery mechanism for that expectation, not itself the proof. New this pass: 8 of 8 booking-category apps surveyed (Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook, Trip.com, Turo, Air New Zealand, Tripadvisor, Shopee) show zero exceptions, a single unstacked back chevron at the exact surface (detail/confirmation) the law governs. Grounds "global Header IS the back; pages add none; focused flows keep theirs" (project_single_global_back memory) as the correct scope: a booking wizard is allowed its own local back precisely because it behaves as a self-contained sub-flow, matching heuristic 4's own scope limit.

**Wayfinding vocabulary (CONV, Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City, 1960).** Paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks: the origin concept for "always know where you are," transferred to digital UX as analogy (NN/g's own "You Are Here" framing), never an independently tested UI claim. Use only as naming vocabulary (a title is a landmark, a breadcrumb is a path, a tab bar is a set of districts), never as a standalone justification for a depth number.

**Contrast case, explicitly not adopted.** Gopuff's per-item colored status chips ("COLD" pills over icons) and Burger King's badge-heavy tab labels ("New" pills, reward icons) were observed in the same scouting pass. These are the decorative/hype-badge pattern Solen's design contract already bans (no fabricated status pips, ink-only CTA, no per-category color); noted here only as the contrast case proving the calm, breadcrumb-free single-back pattern is the one actually aligned with Solen's restraint, not as a pattern to import.

BOUNDARY: this domain governs structural navigation decisions (depth, breadcrumb presence, back-button singularity, tab-bar visibility, label-as-scent). It does not cover the psychological or behavioral half of navigation (habit formation via a persistent tab, reminder cadence, why users return to a surface); those stay in PSYCHOLOGY.md and are not duplicated here.

**Open item for QUESTIONS.md, not a decision made here:** whether Solen's breadcrumb-depth literal should eventually align to NN/g's 3+ floor given the near-unanimous zero-breadcrumb-in-transactional-flow finding across 13 real apps, or whether the app-register substitution argument is sufficient to keep it at 2+. This synthesis does not recommend a change, per the no-reopen constraint on locked literals; it recommends the question be logged with this evidence attached.

synth.taste_lab_probe: Not required to land this section (tag is net-new, a sourced RATIONALE domain, not a generative-gap numeric default). If the team later wants to test the one open question this synthesis surfaces, whether Solen's 2+-level breadcrumb threshold should move to NN/g's 3+ floor given the 13-app zero-breadcrumb convergence, that is a locked-literal change requiring an explicit owner call, and could be probed with a small before/after on a genuine 3-level path (if one exists in Solen's IA) versus the current 2-level category>salon path, watching session recordings for "lost" signals rather than a synthetic lab test.

myths_caught: Airbnb's cited "6-level breadcrumb (Home > All topics > Searching and booking > Booking places to stay > Booking basics > Booking split stays)" is not a verified capture. Mobbin spot-check of Airbnb's actual Help Center found 5-level breadcrumbs on different topics (Home/All topics/Legal terms/Privacy Policy/Airbnb Privacy; Home/All topics/Payments, pricing and refunds/Paying for a reservation/When you'll pay for your reservation), and a search for the exact 'Searching and booking > Booking places to stay > Booking basics > Booking split stays' path returned no matching screen. The general finding (a deep breadcrumb exists only inside Help Center, never the transactional booking flow) held up under spot-check, but the specific 6-level path text reads as an invented illustrative example dressed as an observed screen capture. Softened in verified_addition.

The "three-tap rule" attributed to UXPin could not be confirmed: the most likely URL (uxpin.com/studio/blog/three-tap-rule/) returned 404. The broader point, that a tap/click-count folklore rule circulates with no data behind it, parallel to Porter's already-debunked three-click rule, is plausible and consistent with the domain's own skepticism, but the specific UXPin attribution is unverified in this pass. Softened in verified_addition to not assert a confirmed source.
verified.residual_risks:
Owner-decision item correctly left open (not decided here, per the no-reopen constraint on locked literals): whether Solen's breadcrumb-depth threshold (locked at 2+ levels, SOURCE.md:1229) should move toward NN/g's 3+ no-breadcrumb-needed floor, given the 13-app zero-breadcrumb-in-transactional-flow convergence. The draft correctly proposes logging this to QUESTIONS.md rather than auto-applying; that stands.

Coverage risk on the CONV-tier competitor claims: this verify pass spot-checked 3 of the 13-plus apps cited via Mobbin (Fresha bottom-tab count = 3, confirmed exactly: Home/Search/Calendar; Klook bottom-tab count = 5, confirmed exactly: Home/Destinations/Deals/Trips/Account; Airbnb breadcrumb-confined-to-Help-Center pattern, confirmed in general shape though not the specific 6-level example, see myths_caught). The remaining apps (Treatwell, Booksy, Vagaro, Doctolib, Viator, GetYourGuide, Trip.com, Turo, Air New Zealand, Tripadvisor, Shopee, monday.com, Headspace Support, Zara, H&M, Anthropologie, DICK'S, Target, Amazon, Walmart, Gopuff, Swiggy, Burger King) were not independently re-checked in this pass. The tier is already honestly CONV (not inflated to T1/T2), so no correction is required, but the \"zero of 13\" and \"8 of 8\" phrasing should be read as directional convergence from a single research pass, not a controlled or independently replicated count. If this domain becomes load-bearing for a locked-literal change (the breadcrumb threshold above), a fuller independent re-verification of the full app set is warranted before that decision.

All nine formal academic/industry sources in sources[] were independently verified against primary or near-primary records (CrossRef for the two journal citations, NN/g's own pages for its three guideline citations, direct fetch of the original UIE/CenterCentre three-click study for Porter's exact numbers) and all matched the draft's claimed magnitudes and tiers exactly. No entry required a tier demotion, and none of the draft's numbers_used collide with the myth_screen never-cite table (checked against all ten entries: none of \"2,000% samples\", \"70-90% never change defaults\", \"losses hurt 2x\", jam-study fewer-options, \"$300M button\"/ASOS, \"5%25-95%\" retention-profit, \"5-25x cheaper\" acquisition, \"Amazon 100ms=1%\", Duolingo \"+20% DAU\", or \"UGC 4x\" appear in this draft). This is the strongest-sourced stream reviewed so far in this pass: the fabrication caught is a single illustrative example, not a load-bearing number.
